title: Kuujjuaq’s former elders’ home to undergo repairs before shelter opens
content:
Kuujjuaq’s former Tusaajiapik elders’ home will undergo repairs so it can safely accommodate the community’s homeless population, but it still won’t meet the standards required for a long-term care home, Nunavik health officials say.




Before the building opens as a temporary shelter, valves in its heating system will be replaced, the Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services said in an email that communications co-ordinator Yentl Béliard-Joseph sent to Nunatsiaq News on Tuesday.




To do so, the heating system will need to be shut off for five days.




In April, the health board and Ungava Tulattavik Health Center cited problems with the building’s heating system and other “major technical components.” As a result, the organizations relocated residents to Montreal and closed the home.




On Friday, Deputy Mayor Claude Gadbois told Nunatsiaq News an agreement between the municipality, housing bureau, health board and health centre will allow the building to be used as a homeless shelter until October 2027.




He also said the building does not have a functioning sprinkler system.




Following a 2014 fire at a seniors’ home in L’Isle-Verte that killed 32 people, Quebec introduced requirements for automatic sprinkler systems in seniors’ residences housing 10 or more people. The deadline for facilities to comply was extended to December 2027.

title: Safety a concern in Pangnirtung after increase in RCMP calls: MLA
content:

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: NTI commits $40.8M in federal funding toward health initiatives
content:
Over the next five years, Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. is committing $40.8 million in federal funding to support health and wellness programs.




The organization made the announcement Oct. 21 in a news release.




The funding covers April 1, 2027 to March 31, 2032, and is intended to close the “gap in health outcomes between Inuit and other Canadians,” according to the release.




Nunatsiaq News has requested a copy of the full five-year spending plan from NTI but has not received a response.




In Iqaluit, the Umingmak child and youth advocacy centre and the Piruqatigiit Resource Centre, which provides support to those with fetal alcohol spectrum disorders and other conditions, are among those that will receive an unspecified amount of money.




As well, an unspecified portion of money is earmarked for Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre’s Inunnguiniq childrearing and parenting training program, as well as its Makimautiksat Youth Camp, which aims to promote wellness by getting those aged nine to 12 out on the land.




NTI’s board of directors approved three other spending plans earlier this month aimed at strengthening Inuktut language training and advancing the elimination of tuberculosis.

Kuujjuaq’s shuttered elders’ home is set to become a temporary homeless shelter weeks after the facility’s former residents were

A one-year agreement between the municipality, Nunavik Housing Bureau, Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services and Ungava Tulattavik Health Center will allow the former Tusaajiapik Elders Home building to be used as a homeless shelter until October 2027, deputy Mayor Claude Gadbois said Friday in an interview.




The arrangement comes as the municipality looks for a permanent solution for people who experience homelessness.




Kuujjuaq’s previous homeless shelter closed in September because of its poor condition, including a leaking roof, mould in some areas and recurring leaks caused by problems such as frozen pipes, Gadbois said.




Those who used the shelter have been staying in tents set up behind the building.




“It’s been deteriorating for many years. We kept up with it, but it’s getting to the point where it’s not feasible anymore,” Gadbois said.

The Canadian Coast Guard is preparing to test the Arctic surveillance capacity of a large Israeli-manufactured drone.




Coast guard staff began testing the Hermes 900 Starliner earlier this year at the Canadian Forces Base in Greenwood, N.S., before it was disassembled and shipped from there to Iqaluit on Oct. 1.




The testing will part of an effort to study whether the drone can fit well into the coast guard’s fleet of smaller drones, said Mark McKeeman, the director of the coast guard’s remotely piloted aircraft program.




“Were still in the contract delivery stages with the manufacturer, so they have to prove that the aircraft is capable of operating in some of the conditions in the Arctic,” he said.




One of the things the Hermes 900 Starliner will be tested for is its ability to operate at 72 degrees north, which is about the same latitude as Pond Inlet.




Canada signed a contract to obtain the drone from the Israeli arms dealer Elbit Systems in 2020, at a cost of $36 million.




Transport Canada was initially assigned to manage its use as part of Canada’s National Aerial Surveillance Program, which was transferred over to the coast guard on April 1.

title: Horror writer Jamesie Fournier shares scares in print and on screen
content:
Horror author Jamesie Fournier says he enjoys scaring children almost as much as they enjoy being scared.




“It’s very entertaining to be terrified,” he said Saturday in an interview in his Inhabit Media office in Iqaluit. “That’s why we love horror.”




The Inuktitut and English writer had just launched his latest children’s book,

 Lemming’s First Halloween

, earlier that day at Nunatta Sunakkutaangit Museum.




Dozens of costumed children and their families dropped by the event to create creepy crafts and hear spooky stories.




The book is Fournier’s second in the series. He published 

Lemming’s First Christmas

 in English and Inuktitut in 2024. 

Lemming’s First Halloween 

marks Fournier’s first collaboration with Toronto-based Pakistani-Canadian illustrator Faiza Khan.




The tale follows Lemming and her pup as they cross paths with a qallupilluk, a monster known to drag children into the ocean.




Overcoming fear is an important life skill that Inuit horror stories tap into, Fournier said.
















“When you’re afraid you’re aware of your surroundings. You’re taking everything in. You’re being very cautious. Survivalism has kicked in,” he said. “To be brave we have to first know what scares us.”

author: Randi Beers
title: Jimmy Bell – An Arctic trader
content:
Young Jimmy Bell stood 5’10” tall and weighed about 170 pounds when he joined the Hudson’s Bay Co. as a 19-year-old recruit in 1925. 




Two decades later his weight had more than doubled, by some reports reaching 350 pounds. The Inuit, whom he knew and loved, and who knew and loved him, called him Quinijuq – the fat man.




Bell was born in Cromdale, Scotland, the eldest son in a large family. He walked three miles to school and back each day during eight years of primary school and followed that with three years of higher education. 




Then Bell worked as a bookkeeper for a local garage for three years until he emigrated to Canada as a young fur trader, following in the footsteps of so many young Scots before him. 




Montreal, the city where he first set foot in Canada, was always dear to him. Much later, he decided that he would eventually retire there, but it was never to be.




That summer of 1925 he travelled on the Hudson’s Bay Company supply ship to Lake Harbour (now Kimmirut) where he was apprentice clerk for three years, before moving on to Frobisher Bay for two years in the same position. 




After a year’s furlough, Bell was posted for one year as manager at Payne Bay in northern Quebec, a post he described as the poorest-looking he had seen. He followed that with two years each again in Frobisher Bay and Lake Harbour. 
















After another year of furlough, Bell returned to Lake Harbour for another five years, before spending short periods at the Winnipeg Depot and Cross Lake, Man. Then he spent four years, from 1942 to 1946, as manager in Arctic Bay. 




After a short holiday, Bell returned for a fourth tour of duty at Lake Harbour, only a year this time, before transferring to Cape Dorset for his final year in the Arctic and his final year of life.




Bell loved Arctic Bay, the company’s most northerly post. He was a sociable man, a good cook and a gracious host. Visitors were always welcome, whether they be other traders, missionaries, policemen, or Inuit. He liked to eat, drink, play bridge, and tell stories. 




Yet one sketch of his life says, “Those he liked thought he was wonderful. Those who didn’t found him dour and reserved.”




Bell had an enormous appetite and it was said that he could eat eight to 10 pounds of seal meat at one sitting. There was a Department of Transport weather station in Arctic Bay and Bell got in the habit of visiting for Sunday supper, bringing “his huge bulk and fund of stories.”




All post managers were required to keep a daily journal and a monthly summary of their journals. For some, it was a sparse record of the comings and goings of the Inuit to the post to trade, usually with remarks on the weather. But Bell’s journals were more than that. 
















Rather than just a bare record of trading activities, he took time to write in detail about the visits of the Inuit and observances of nature. They were carefully written and showed a love of language. 




In May of 1944 he wrote, “The first snow-birds of the season were observed on the 10

th

, which is almost three weeks later than their first appearance last year. These hardy little birds must still find the Arctic nights rather chilly.” 




Bell showed the same care when writing about the Inuit. 




That same month, when Tonga died at Cape Cunningham, he wrote, “He was the oldest native in the territory and we believe the last of the ‘Angakoks’… [H]e was the last strong link with paganism. We think, however, that the old man’s brand of pagan religion was just as good as that taught by the Missionaries; at least Tonga was less deceitful than some of his brethren who have seen the ‘light.’”  




Such detail in a journal is all the more remarkable when one realizes that probably no one other than his district manager in Winnipeg would read his words at the time. 
















Bell’s Hudson’s Bay Company service record describes him as a “good reliable type,” and a “first class Eskimo trader.” One report called him a “permanent Arctic man,” but noted ominously that he was “dangerously obese.” 




Bell loved his drink. He spent Christmas Day 1933 at Frobisher Bay working, and wrote, “Christmas Day was spent in the store, where 83 foxes were traded. At night I celebrated Xmas by having a fire in the guardroom [sitting room] and having a better meal than usual. I also put up with the torture of a collar and tie, and toasted the health of absent friends in lime juice; not that it was necessary to do so, as I have three kinds of strong drink on the post, but there is no pleasure in drinking alone, although in company I can hold my own.” 




At Arctic Bay, he and his clerk hosted the staff of the Met station, as the weather station was called, for New Year’s dinner in 1944. 




“We had a first class meal,” Bell wrote, “which consisted of… mushroom soup, roast pork with apple sauce, carrots, peas, mashed potatoes, ice cream with strawberries, coffee and cake. Prior to the meal by way of appetizers the usual toasts were drunk in beer and ‘Nelson’s Blood.’” 




Nelson’s Blood was a euphemism for Lamb’s Navy rum. He also liked another cocktail of rum and port, a “smooth tasting concoction” that he called “thunder and lightning.” 




Bell also tended to the illnesses of the Inuit, pulling teeth and even amputating frozen fingers. 




Elsie Gillis, who spent a year in Arctic Bay as the wife of a weather observer, wrote of Bell, “When they [the Inuit] were in trouble, they came to him for help and he gave generously of his time, his skill, his food. Or whatever was needed to meet the emergency.”  




My next column will tell about how Bell became the ghost of Arctic Bay.




Taissumani is an occasional column that recalls events of historical interest. Kenn Harper is a historian and writer who lived in the Arctic for over 50 years. He is the author of 

Give Me Winter, Give Me Dogs: Knud Rasmussen and the Fifth Thule Expedition

, and 

Thou Shalt Do No Murder

, among other books. Feedback? Send your comments and questions to kennharper@hotmail.com.

title: Housing, homelessness in focus in Ottawa’s Rideau-Vanier race
content:
Six candidates are vying to represent Ottawa’s Rideau-Vanier ward ahead of next week’s municipal election, with housing, homelessness and support for the Inuit community among campaign issues.




Ottawans are set to elect ward councillors Monday to a four-year term. Rideau-Vanier includes Vanier, sometimes called “Little Nunavut,” home to an urban Inuit community.




Statistics Canada counted 1,270 Inuit in Ottawa in the 2021 census.




Lyra Evans, Julie Fiala Chartrand, Brian Paquette and Michael Karl Sewanaku spoke with Nunatsiaq News about issues that could impact Inuit residents in the ward.




Evans, a former Ottawa-Carleton District School Board trustee and chair, said residents have raised concerns about homelessness, addiction, poverty and food insecurity.




“Pushing people out of a park and destroying all their belongings doesn’t stop them from being homeless,” Evans said, criticizing the city’s approach to encampments.




For more than 30 years, the Rideau-Sussex pedestrian underpass has served as a gathering place for unhoused Inuit. Police patrols, tickets and removals over the summer have

“It’s important for parents to take this very seriously. This program is for the students’ well being,” she said.




Aloupa said the initiative responds to a need raised by Nunavik residents and parents. The school board’s council of commissioners heard a presentation from the health board about the proposed program in June.




The program will cover students from kindergarten to Grade 11, with information packages for different age groups.

title: Man dies after being struck by vehicle near Ullivik health centre
content:
A 69-year-old man is dead after being struck by a driver near the Ullivik health centre in Dorval, Que., on Tuesday.




The incident happened near the health centre after a driver turned from Orly Avenue onto Michel-Jasmin Avenue, said Montreal police spokesperson Raphaël Bergeron in an interview with Nunatsiaq News.




On Wednesday, Ullivik director Rita Novalinga, Inuulitsivik Health Centre executive director Sarah Beaulne and Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services executive director Jennifer Munick-Watkins issued a statement about “the tragic death of a member of our community last night in Dorval.”




“As a community, we mourn this loss together,” the statement reads. “Our thoughts and hearts are with the family, loved ones, and the entire Inukjuak community during this difficult time.”




The statement did not provide any more details about the incident, and NRBHSS, which issued the statement, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.




Other fatal collisions have happened near the health centre. In 2022, two Inuit women, in two separate incidents, were killed by drivers on nearby Highway 520.

ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᐅᔪᑦ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᓕᖅᐳᑦ ᐅᓄᙱᓐᓂᖅᓴᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒎᔪᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒧᑦ-ᐱᔾᔪᑎᓕᖕᓂ ᑐᒃᓯᕋᐅᑕᐅᔪᓂ ᐊᔪᖅᑎᑕᐅᓕᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐅᕘᓇ ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᐅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᓯᒪᔪᒥᑦ.




ᒐᕙᒪᑐᖃᒃᑯᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᔪᖅ, ᐊᔾᔨᐸᓗᐊᓂ ᔪᐊᑕᓐ ᑐᙵᕕᐅᔪᒥ, ᓴᓇᓯᒪᕗᖅ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᓱᕈᓯᕐᓂ ᑲᓇᑕᓕᒫᒥ ᓇᓕᒧᑦᑐᒥ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ, ᐃᓅᖃᑎᒌᖕᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᐅᔪᓂ.




2024-25−ᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᖓᓂ, ᐃᓄᐃᑦ ᓱᕈᓰᑦ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᐅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᓯᒪᔪᑦ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᖅᑎᑦᑎᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᓄᓇᕘᑉ 27−ᖑᔪᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐊᑭᓕᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᑮᓇᐅᔾᔭᒃᓴᓂᐅᔪᓂ 88−ᓄᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᑲᐃᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᓂ. ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑏᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᓕᓵᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᖁᑦᑎᒃᑐᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᓂᑦ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓇᐃᓴᐅᑎᓂ ᑐᓂᔭᐅᔪᓂ ᓄᓇᑦᑎᓯᐊᖅ ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓄᑦ ᓄᓇᕘᑉ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ.




ᐊᕐᕌᓂ, ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ 75−ᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᑲᐃᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᓂ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᖃᖅᑎᖓ ᑲᑐᓚ ᒪᑦᓴᓯ ᖃᕋᓴᐅᔭᑎᒍᑦ ᑎᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ.




ᐅᖃᕈᒪᓚᐅᙱᓚᖅ ᖃᔅᓯᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᑲᐃᓐᓇᖅᑐᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐅᔪᓂ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒎᔪᒥ. ᐃᒪᓐᓇᖔᖅ, ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᓯᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ “ᑭᒡᓕᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐅᓄᕐᓂᐅᔪᓂ.”




“ᑕᐃᓐᓇ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᑦᑎᐊᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᓄᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᒥ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖓ ᔭᔅᑎᓐ ᒫᑦᓯᑦ ᐊᐱᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ, “ᐊᒥᓱᓂ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᓂᑦ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ ᑖᔅᓱᒥᖓ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᖄᒃᑲᓐᓂᐊᒍᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᓂ.”
















ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᓴᓇᔨᓂᑦ ᐃᓚᐅᖃᑕᐅᕗᑦ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕐᕕᐊᕈᓯᕐᒥ ᐃᓕᓴᐃᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐃᑲᔪᕐᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᕈᑎᒃᓴᓂ, ᐱᓗᐊᖅᑐᒥ ᑕᐅᑐᒃᑕᑐᐊᖃᑲᐃᓐᓇᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐃᓕᓐᓂᐊᖅᑎᓄᑦ ᐱᔭᕆᐊᓕᖕᓂ ᐊᓯᐊᒎᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᓄᑦ.

title: QEC announces planned power outages in Kimmirut, Resolute Bay

Qulliq Energy Corp. is planning outages in Kimmirut and Resolute Bay this weekend, with the possibility of an outage in Iqaluit as well.




The corporation announced the outages in a series of public service announcements Thursday as it gears up for a weekend of work.




In Resolute Bay, QEC is carrying out maintenance on the power lines to get them ready for winter. A planned outage is set to take place Saturday and Sunday from 7 a.m. to 11 a.m. to allow for this work.




In Kimmirut, QEC is installing a new generator in the hamlet’s power plant. An outage is scheduled for Sunday, from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Makivvik wants to end time changes in Nunavik — but eyes next year for it
content:
People across Nunavik will be changing their clocks when daylight saving time ends on Nov. 1.




This is a pivot from Makivvik’s earlier plans, announced Oct. 30, 2025, for Nunavik to stay on daylight saving time year-round, starting this year.




Technical and administrative issues prevented the move, Makivvik announced Oct. 14 in a news release.




Now, the organization that represents Inuit across Nunavik is targeting November 2027 to end seasonal time changes in the region.




Makivvik launched a survey in January 2025 that asked Nunavimmiut whether the region should abolish seasonal time changes and, if so, whether it should remain on daylight saving time or standard time.




The clocks move forward during daylight saving time, creating more daylight hours in the evening, but later sunrises. Standard time brings earlier sunrises, but earlier sunsets too.




The organization said it will continue working through the legal and practical steps needed to make the change, the release said.
















Clocks will move forward again on March 14, 2027, when daylight saving time resumes, the release said.

Joshua often walked to unwind after work, sometimes stopping at a nearby convenience store.

Brenda said she later retraced the route herself in April, walking to the spot where his body was discovered, about 600 metres from their Vanier neighbourhood home.

title: Casual student support staff approvals in Nunavut drops from 75 to 15
content:
Nunavut’s Education Department approved 15 requests for casual student support assistants this school year, one-fifth of the number it approved the school year prior.




Of those 15, a total of 11 have been hired, according to figures the department provided Nunatsiaq News Wednesday.




The department is recruiting workers for the remaining four positions, spokesperson Kuthula Matshazi said in an email.




He said some positions couldn’t get filled despite recruiting efforts. Others remained vacant due to relief employees filling in or workers going on leave.




Student support workers join classroom teachers to help them deliver the curriculum. They work with individual students who require accommodations and those who follow unique education guidelines. School leaders can submit requests for casual support staff when they don’t have enough permanent staff to meet demand.

title: City closer to approving $216M budget for infrastructure in 2027
content:
Water infrastructure and related upgrades make up more than half of the City of Iqaluit’s proposed $216-million capital budget for 2027.




Wastewater system upgrades soak up more than $80 million of the budget. Water infrastructure accounts for another $75 million, which includes $38 million for raw water intake, supply and storage.




Peter Tumilty, the city’s chief financial officer, introduced the proposed budget to councillors during Tuesday’s governance and priorities committee meeting. He began his presentation with an explanation as to why this year’s proposed budget is 

more than double

 last year’s $90-million capital plan.




“We have elected this year to show the entire cost of the project in the current year rather than spreading it out over the life of the project based on expected annual spending,” Tumilty said.




In the past, the city has spread project costs over multiple years to minimize the impact on the city’s finances, he said. This year, projects that are fully or substantially funded by third parties, such as the federal government, are fully costed into the budget.




For example, the city is planning to spend $60 million on wastewater system 

upgrades

 next year with money from the federal Building Canada Strong Fund.




This improves the city’s ability to plan multi-year projects and to optimize sealift scheduling, Tumilty said.

title: Video game helps Inuit youth learn mental wellness strategies
content:
When Letia Kalluk wrote her song 

Maana

In 

Virtual Qaggiq

“The lyrics go something like, ‘A wise man told me that you’re still young. You have a lot to live for. You haven’t seen the whole world yet,’” said Kalluk, who is from Arctic Bay, in an interview.




“It’s really good for [youth] to hear music in their own language. It’s been very fulfilling for me as an artist to contribute to that.”




York University researchers, Inuit youth and cultural advisers started developing the game in 2022.




It follows Alaasua, the main character, through seven quests that pair Inuit cultural activities with mental wellness strategies, said project co-ordinator Yogita Singh.




In one quest, mythical creatures tempt Alaasua to drink spoiled water while she gathers fresh water and ice. Players learn to resist the temptation and manage stress without turning to substance use, Singh said.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit deputy mayor calls on police foot patrols to resume
content:
Iqaluit’s deputy mayor is calling for “very successful” joint patrols between Iqaluit bylaw and RCMP to be reinstated, after the project was halted in the spring due to a lack of available police officers.




“I would like to call on the RCMP to get their staffing numbers to where we can work together again,” said Kim Smith during Tuesday’s governance and priorities meeting. 

“It was very successful and we definitely saw a difference in the city.”




The pilot project ran from January through March. It ended due to a lack of available police officers, said Iqaluit’s chief municipal enforcement officer Steven Allen Tuesday during a presentation to the committee.




“While the project was in motion, it was a success, but the RCMP was unable to sustain providing a member for this project due to staffing levels,” Allen said.




Both agencies provided one officer each to patrol together daily in the afternoons. They focused on traffic-related offences and public intoxication, he said.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: John Amagoalik scholarship recipient calls win motivating
content:
Nunavut Sivuniksavut student Jamie Comeau is the winner of this year’s $10,000 John Amagoalik scholarship.




Qikiqtani Inuit Association announced winner Oct. 16 in a news release.




“With this scholarship, it gives me more motivation to keep going into universities after second year, so much more motivation to come to school and do better,” Comeau said in an interview.




The John Amagoalik scholarship scholarship is presented to an Inuk student who is pursuing journalism or studies that promote Inuit language and culture. This year QIA doubled its value from $5,000 to $10,000.




After graduating from Inuksuk High School in Iqaluit, Comeau enrolled in Nunavut Sivuniksavut, an Ottawa-based college program for Inuit.




She graduated her first year of Inuit Studies with honours and an award for her dedication to learning Inuktitut. Now in her second year, Comeau is studying Advanced Inuit Studies.




“I feel a little more at ease when it comes to financial stability. Last year I was struggling,” she said, adding that the scholarship allows her to enjoy the south and focus on her education rather than stress about affording food and housing.
















After graduating from Nunavut Sivuniksavut, Comeau plans to attend Carleton University in Ottawa, though she’s unsure of which program. She says she wants to finish her education at Dalhousie University in Halifax.

title: New Inuk recruit talks benefits, challenges of policing in his hometown
content:
Cst. Jerry Patterson has always wanted to follow in his father’s footsteps. 




His father Allen Patterson served as a police officer with the Kativik Regional Police, now known as the Nunavik Police Service, for seven years.




“I spent my entire youth watching my dad be a cop,” Jerry Patterson said. “It inspired me to pursue that path.”




Now, Patterson is one of three Inuit officers in the Nunavik Police Service, which is 

working to increase

 Inuit recruitment. 




The number of Inuit officers has remained at three since at least last year, despite the hiring of Patterson in July, due to another Inuk officer who left the service a few months ago and has since taken a position with another police service.




Patterson works two-week rotations in his hometown of Umiujaq, as well as in Puvirnituq.




 Knowing people in his hometown has sometimes been an advantage in de-escalating tense situations, Patterson said.

At the same time, there have also been people who have reacted aggressively toward Patterson because of their existing relationship, but he said he doesn’t view these encounters as a negative.

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Gjoa Haven journalism student wants more Inuit telling their own stories
content:
Gjoa Haven resident Emerald Hatkaittuq is pursuing a career she has thought about since high school.





































The 23-year-old is one of the first two Inuit students enrolled in Carleton University’s Certificate in Journalism in Indigenous Communities. The nine-month program, designed to train Indigenous journalists to tell stories from their own communities, is in its second year.




“Representation is so important. When applications opened for this year, I shared it with people I know because I want to see more Inuit pursuing journalism,” said Hatkaittuq.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut Health Department warns of federal cheese recall
content:
The Government of Nunavut is warning about 

another

 cheese product recall issued by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency due to listeria contamination.




Issued by the federal agency on Oct. 14, the recall is for

 12 organic cheeses by Farm Boy, L’Ancêtre and Life Smart, with expiry dates that range from Dec. 4, 2026, to July 30, 2027.




They include Swiss, cheddar, mozza-cheddar and mozzarella products.




The territorial Health Department shared the warning with Nunavummiut Monday in a public service announcement.




Listeria monocytogenes is bacteria that causes a type of infection known as listeriosis. It can cause vomiting, fever, muscle aches, headaches and neck stiffness.




Contaminated food may not appear spoiled, but it can still cause sickness, the announcement said. Nunavummiut should throw out recalled products or return it to the store they bought it from.




Pregnant women, elders and residents with compromised immune systems are particularly at risk, according to the federal agency’s statement.
















The agency is investigating the source of the contamination and more recalls may follow, the agency’s website states.




The Canadian Food Inspection Agency issued a recall in September for Coaticook’s aged cheddar cheese, with a best before date of Aug. 3, also due to listeria contamination.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Alleged Pangnirtung shooter makes first court appearance
content:
RCMP officers are working to pull together witness accounts and videos taken of an incident earlier this month in Pangnirtung that led to a man being shot.




At around 4 p.m. on Oct. 6, RCMP 

received reports

 of gunshots within the community. Jonah Kuniliusie, 21, was arrested shortly after and taken into custody.




Kuniliusie 

faces several charges

, including two counts of endangering life, two counts of pointing a firearm, two counts of aggravated assault, and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon in public.




He also faces three counts related to breaching probation.




Kuniliusie made his first appearance virtually in an Iqaluit courtroom Tuesday.




During the brief, two-minute appearance the Crown told the court that RCMP estimated it would take approximately one month to pull together witness statements and video.




Kuniliusie’s next court date is scheduled for Nov. 17.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Families seek answers after Nunavik elders home residents relocated to Montreal
content:
Alaku Kululaa says she was shocked to learn her 90-year-old mother would be relocated south after building issues forced the closure of Kuujjuaq’s Tusaajiapik elders home this fall.




Originally from Quaqtaq, Louisa Inuluk Kululaa had been living at the home for approximately three years.




Alaku Kululaa said she received no written notice about the decision and that the head nurse instead verbally informed her in mid-September, about two weeks before the move was scheduled to take place.




On Sept. 30, Louisa Inuluk Kululaa was checked into the Argyle care home, located in the Montreal suburb of Point-Claire, about 1,500 kilometres away from Kuujjuaq.




“I feel so far away from her,” Alaku Kululaa said. “It is stressful not knowing how she is. Without communication, how could I know?”




Problems at the Tusaajiapik elders home have been persistent since April, when Nunavik health officials 

announced

 there were technical issues with the building’s heating system. With cold weather setting in this fall, the facility is closed and officials are 

working

 to assess the cost and feasibility of fixing the problem.




Now, families are calling for better communication and assurances there will be culturally appropriate care and support for their loved ones in the south.

author: Daron Letts
title: Iqaluit RCMP investigate elders’ van vandalism
content:
RCMP are investigating after vandals targeted the Iqaluit Elders Home Sunday.




Officers responded to a report Sunday shortly after 6:30 p.m. about rocks being thrown at the elder’s facility and the van. The incident resulted in a broken window in the van used by the home to transport residents.




The van’s broken window had been temporarily repaired with tape on Monday.




If no suspects are identified, the investigation will be concluded, RCMP spokesperson Sgt. George Henrie said in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




The file can be reopened if police receive new information, he added.




The Nunavut government-run elders home is located on Queen Elizabeth II Way and has eight beds for seniors who require lower levels of assisted care.




Staff at the home declined to comment.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Iqaluit woman charged with 2nd-degree murder
content:
RCMP have charged a woman with second-degree murder following a disturbance in Iqaluit’s Tundra Valley neighbourhood over the weekend.




Police found a 37-year-old woman with life threatening injuries in the city’s 2400 block at around 5:50 a.m. on Saturday, said RCMP spokesperson Sgt. George Henrie in a news release.




She was transported to Qikiqtani General hospital, where she died.




Christie Nutarariaq, 32, has been charged with second degree murder in relation to the incident.




The incident is unrelated to 

another

 murder charge that police announced Monday.




In that case, RCMP charged a 21-year-old Qaqasie Aningmiuq with second-degree murder, following an altercation on Oct. 6 that left one man dead.




Nutarariaq is in custody. Her next court appearance is set for Nov. 17.

title: Man charged with murder following Oct. 6 altercation that left another man dead
content:
RCMP have charged a man with second-degree murder in connection with an altercation that happened Oct. 6 in Iqaluit.




Qaqasie Aningmiuq, 21, was arrested on Oct. 16, Nunavut RCMP said Monday in a news release issued by Sgt. George Henrie.




Police previously 

identified

 the man who died as 38-year-old Robert Kipanik.

ᑕᓪᓕᒪᓂ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᐅᔪᓂ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑐᓂ $1 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᐃᓄᓕᒫᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖏᓐᓂ ᓱᓕ ᐅᖅᑯᑎᒦᙱᓚᑦ ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᕐᒥ ᐊᖅᑯᑎᒦᓐᓇᑎᒃ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᓯᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᑕᐃᒪᐃᑦᑐᒥ ᐱᔨᖅᑎᕋᕐᓂᐅᔪᒥ.




ᑐᓂᓯᔪᓐᓇᙱᑎᓪᓗᒍ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᖅᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓂ ᖃᖓ ᐱᔭᕇᖅᓯᒪᔭᕆᐊᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓄᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓚᕆᖕᓂᖓᓂ, ᓯᕗᓕᖅᑎ ᔮᓐ ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ “ᐱᔪᒪᓂᕆᕙᖓ” ᑕᑯᓂᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᒃᑲᓐᓂᕐᓂᖏᓐᓂ 2027−ᒥ — ᐊᕐᕌᒍᑦ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᖄᖏᖅᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᓂᐅᕕᖅᑕᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋᑦ.




“ᓄᑖᙳᕆᐊᖅᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓ, ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒥ, ᓱᓕ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᙱᑦᑐᖅ,” ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᖃᓘᑎᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐱᖅᓱᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 9−ᒥ. “ᑭᓯᐊᓂ, ᒐᕙᒪᕗᑦ ᒪᓕᒍᒪᐅᑎᖃᙱᓚᑦ ᐆᒧᖓ.”




ᐱᓕᕆᐊᒃᓴᖅ ᓄᖅᑲᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ 2025−ᒥ, ᐃᓱᐊᓂ ᓯᕗᓂᐊᓂ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᑦ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᓂᖏᓐᓂ, ᐱᔾᔪᑎᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᑕᖃᙱᓗᐊᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓂᖓᓄᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᓂ ᐊᑐᖅᑕᐅᔪᒃᓴᐅᑕᐅᔪᓂ.




ᑕᒪᓐᓇ ᐊᓯᔾᔨᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᐱᕐᙶᖅ 2026−ᒥ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᖅᑏᑦ ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓕᒐᓕᐅᕐᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᖏᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒋ $1.25 ᒥᓕᐊᓐᓂ ᖄᒃᑲᓐᓂᐊᒍᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ, ᒪᐃᓐ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ.




ᐸᓯᒥ ᐱᔨᑦᑎᕋᕐᓂᖅ ᓯᕗᓪᓕᖅᐹᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓯᕗᓂᒃᓴᒧᑦ ᐊᔪᙱᓐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᐱᓕᒻᒪᒃᓴᓂᕐᒥ ᓕᒥᑎᒃᑯᓐᓂᑦ, ᐊᒻᒪ ᑐᒃᑐ ᑖᒃᓯᓂᑦ.
















ᐊᑕᐅᓯᕐᒥ ᓄᓇᓯᐅᑎᖃᖅᐳᑦ ᐊᑐᓂ ᑕᓪᓕᒪᓂ ᓄᓇᓕᐅᔪᓂ: ᐃᖃᓗᐃᑦ, ᐃᖃᓗᒃᑑᑦᑎᐊᖅ, ᑲᖏᖅᖠᓂᖅ, ᓴᓪᓕᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐸᖕᓂᖅᑑᒥ. ᐅᑭᐅᖅᑕᖅᑐᒥ ᓯᕗᓂᒃᓴᒧᑦ ᐊᔪᙱᓐᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᐱᕙᓪᓕᐊᑎᑕᐅᓂᖓᓂ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᒥ, ᓂᐅᕕᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᑮᓇᐅᔭᖃᖅᑎᑕᐅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒻᒥ ᒐᕙᒪᒃᑯᓐᓂ.




ᖁᑉᐸ ᒪᐃᒃ ᓇᖏᖅᐳᖅ ᓴᓂᓕᐊᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ ᐸᓯᖓᓂ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐸᐃᕆᓃᑦ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖏᑦ ᐃᖃᓗᖕᓂ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᑦ’ ᖃᒻᒪᖓᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 9−ᒥ. (ᑎᐊᕆᓐ ᓕᐊᑦᔅ ᐊᔾᔨᖁᑎᖓ)

title: Qikiqtarjuaq man forfeits right to jury trial after sleeping in
content:
A Qikiqtarjuaq man lost his right to a jury trial after he accidentally slept through a court date in early September.




Ronald Audlakiak faces four charges, alleged to have taken place between Nov. 30 and Dec. 5, 2024. They include sexual assault with a weapon, assault involving suffocation, assault and uttering threats.




His four-day jury trial was supposed to begin on the morning of Sept. 1 in Qikiqtarjuaq.




Sixty community members had gathered at Qikiqtarjuaq’s community hall anticipating the start of jury selection, Justice Mark Mossey said in a written decision dated Oct. 15.




When Audlakiak didn’t present himself at court, Mossey delayed the proceedings until the afternoon. He did not give a reason, in an effort to avoid prejudicing the jurors.




Audlakiak then arrived when court reconvened and jury selection proceeded in the afternoon.




The accused once again failed to show up the next morning, for Day 2 of his trial.
















Mossey declared a mistrial, issued an arrest warrant and, an hour later, RCMP found him asleep in his mother’s home.




When court reconvened in the afternoon to determine next steps, Audlakiak said he did not want to give up his right to jury trial and requested a hearing to determine whether that right had been waived.

title: ‘Burnout and hardship’: Nunavut teachers struggle with loss of student support workers
content:
Teachers in Nunavut have access to fewer student support assistants this year after school-related requests became ineligible for funding under the Inuit Child First Initiative.




The federal funding program, similar to Jordan’s Principle, is designed to ensure Inuit children across Canada have equal access to health, social and educational supports.




In the 2024-25 school year, the Inuit Child First Initiative allowed Nunavut’s 27 district education authorities to pay the salaries of 88 casual student support workers. The staff worked in elementary and high schools, according to figures provided to Nunatsiaq News by Nunavut’s Education Department.




Last year, the department approved 75 casual workers, said department spokesperson Kuthula Matshazi in an email.




He declined to say how many casual support workers are working in Nunavut schools this year. Instead, he characterized it as a “limited number.”




“When that funding was readily available,” said Nunavut Teachers Association president Justin Matchett in an interview, “there were a lot of schools that were accessing that and getting additional support staff.”

title: The world is ending, and I feel fine
content:
A friend told me a story this summer about

It wasn’t long ago that wildfire smoke was a characteristic of summer mostly limited to western North America, where conditions are drier.

parts

increased

title: RCMP charge former Kugaaruk hamlet employee with fraud
content:
A former Hamlet of Kugaaruk employee is facing six counts of fraud-related charges, after a year-long RCMP investigation.




Police have charged 29-year-old Hanah Arafiles with fraud over $5,000, forgery, uttering forged documents, drawing document without authority, theft under $5,000 and possession of property obtained by crime.




Sgt. George Henrie announced the charges in a news release on Friday.




In August 2025, police opened an investigation after the hamlet alleged that a former employee had defrauded it earlier that year.




One year later, a Nunavut judge issued an arrest warrant.




On Oct. 8, the Ontario Provincial Police arrested Arafiles in Pembroke, Ont.




She has been released from custody and is scheduled to appear in Iqaluit court on Nov. 2.

title: Judge puts Mary River Mine’s future in hands of neutral decision-makers
content:
Final say over the future of the Mary River iron mine is in the hands of two neutral, court-appointed parties, an Ontario judge has ordered.




Justice Jana Steele’s decision on Oct. 14 comes as Baffinland Iron Mines Corp.

The mine contributes roughly 25 per cent of Nunavut’s gross domestic product.




“At this time, the alternative to a transaction is a liquidation, which would have a devastating impact … including the loss of over 1,200 jobs,” said Steele, a superior court judge.

author: Randi Beers
title: Feeding our family — and the community
content:
Dear Nunatsiaq News,




I am writing to share a story about my father Walter J. Porter of Gjoa Haven, Nunavut, and a tradition of sharing that I have witnessed since I was a girl.




My father is blind, but he remains connected to our Inuit traditions and our community through sharing country food. His son provides him with caribou meat, while other family members help butcher it.




What makes this tradition special is that the meat is for our family, as well as for anybody else. It is placed outside so that community members can take whatever they want. People are welcome to take some home for themselves and their families.




My father is happy to be outside for a while when people gather to collect the meat. There is company outside, and people come and go as they take what they need. It is a simple but meaningful way of bringing people together through sharing.




As far back as I can remember, this has been part of my life. I was little when I first noticed this tradition. My father’s grandchildren now see what sharing means.

title: Esthetician prepares for New York Fashion Week
content:
Odette Wills wasn’t allowed to wear makeup as a teenager.




Now, the 26-year-old Iqaluit esthetician is preparing to work as a makeup artist backstage at New York Fashion Week, from Feb. 12 to 14.




“I still think I have a long way to go,” Wills said during an interview in her new home-based Authentic Glow Studio which opened in May, the product of a New Year’s resolution.




Wills travelled to New York City for a week in September, where she completed a course at Aimakeup Beauty Academy in Westside Manhattan’s Chelsea neighbourhood and 

befriended Instagram influencer Ipek.




“Odette is very talented,” said Aiyma, the school’s founder who goes by one name, in a phone interview Tuesday.




New York Fashion Week, held in February and September every year, features fashion industry shows throughout Manhattan and marks the debut of many international labels.




In the fall, Aiyma’s students (not including Wills) provided makeup for models working with brand labels such as Geo in Style, F&W and Amari Carter, among others. 

In December, Wills will learn what brands she will be working with, Aiyma said.

content:

The school overlooks the community from atop a raised plot of ground next to the airport.

title: Proposed federal lands act amendment could complicate devolution: premier
content:
Ottawa’s tinkering with its Territorial Lands Act could throw a wrench in Nunavut’s devolution work, says Premier John Main.




He was speaking to a

The act governs use of Crown land in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, including its sale or lease,

title: President, community director roles up for grabs in QIA election
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is looking for its next president.




It’s also looking for community directors in Iqaluit, Igloolik, Kimmirut, Sanirajak, Clyde River, Pond Inlet and Sanikiluaq, said a news release issued Thursday by Markoosie Qaunirq, spokesperson for QIA.




Each position carries a four-year term.




The nomination period for the election runs from Nov. 9 to 13.




Eligible voters must be Inuit, enrolled under the Nunavut Agreement; at least 16 years old; and have resided in the Qikiqtani Region for one year or more, according to the release.




The current QIA president Olayuk Akesuk 

won

 the 2022 election over Paul Okalik, with 61.2 per cent of the vote. He had served in the role since the fall of 2021, when he took over from P.J. Akeeagok, who resigned to run for MLA.




Election day is set for Dec. 14.

The Nunavik Regional Board of Health and Social Services announced the partnership Oct. 13 in a news release with Quebec Health Centre-West-of-Montreal University and the Constance-Lethbridge Rehabilitation Centre.




With the initiative, residents will have access to equipment fitting and follow-up care without needing to travel outside the region for some services.




Orthotics are devices, such as braces or specially fitted supports, that help stabilize or protect parts of the body. Prosthetics are artificial limbs or other devices that replace a missing body part. Positioning services involve selecting and adapting equipment, such as wheelchairs, seating systems and other supports.




A technologist specializing in orthotics, prosthetics and orthopedic care will be regularly present in Nunavik, the release said.




Assessments and moulding will be conducted in local communities, allowing patients to receive some services without travelling south.

title: Carpentry to return to Victor Sammurtok School
content:
Woodworking will soon be back on the curriculum at Chesterfield Inlet’s Victor Sammurtok School following a three-year absence.




“There is so much value in a woodshop,” said principal Jacques Theriault during an interview earlier this semester. “With woodworking, we’re introducing a trade and there’s a lifetime career right there.”




The new woodshop is expected to be in operation in time to offer the program to students by mid-January, he added.




The school had a functioning woodshop in the past, but former staff converted the space into a weight room following the COVID-19 pandemic.




The room is still equipped with industrial ventilation and wiring to accommodate the electrical demands of a fully functioning shop.




When 

Theriault became principal in January 2025, he immediately began searching for funders to reinstate the woodshop, though he admired the quality of the weight room, he said.

title: Man dies after altercation in Iqaluit
content:
RCMP are treating the death of a man involved in an altercation in Iqaluit last week as a homicide.




Police responded to calls about an altercation at around 9:55 p.m. on Oct. 6, according to a press release issued Wednesday by Sgt. George Henrie.




Two people were transported to the Qikiqtani General Hospital with life-threatening injuries.




“Despite life saving measures, one male succumbed to his injuries,” Henrie wrote.




RCMP identified the man who died as 38-year-old Robert Kipanik.




The other person, who has yet to be identified, was medivaced to Ottawa, where he is in stable condition.




The RCMP’s Major Crime Unit is investigating.

title: QIA funds $15M wellness centre in Igloolik
content:
A wellness centre planned for Igloolik’s core will be a positive addition to the community, says a hamlet leader.




Last week, the Qikiqtani Inuit Association announced $15 million for the Saviruut Building, which will house hamlet wellness initiatives and a federally funded early childhood development program.




“It’s good to see that we’re getting more infrastructure, because the need is there,” senior administrative officer John Ivey said in an interview with Nunatsiaq News.




The hamlet asked QIA to fund a wellness centre a few years before Ivey joined its administration.




The regional organization, responsible for just over 51 per cent of Nunavut’s Inuit population, allocated the money from its Indigenous Community Infrastructure Fund.

title: Iqaluit crosswalk lights temporarily shut down
content:
Iqaluit’s only controlled 

crosswalk

The lighted crossing is adjacent to the intersection of Niaqungusiariaq Road and Queen Elizabeth Way.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nominations for KIA elections to open Oct. 26
content:
Nominations for five seats on the Kivalliq Inuit Association board of directors will open on Oct. 26.




The election is scheduled for Dec. 14, c

hief returning officer Penny Taylor announced Tuesday, in the association’s notice of election.




The roles include vice-president and secretary/treasurer, as well as the community director positions in Naujaat, Rankin Inlet and Whale Cove.




“This year’s election is more than a procedural milestone — it is an opportunity for Inuit across the Kivalliq region to help shape the future of their communities and strengthen Inuit-led governance,” Taylor said in an email on Tuesday. “

The voices of Inuit voters and nominees are essential to that work.”




The nomination period closes at 3 p.m. on Nov. 9.




Advance polls will be held on Dec. 7, Taylor said.




Mobile polls will also visit schools, elders’ centres, health centres, mine sites, boarding homes, healing facilities, and Winnipeg’s Uquutaq Medical Boarding Home. Schedules for each community will be posted by Nov. 30.
















Eligible voters must be an Inuk enrolled under the Nunavut Agreement aged 16 years or older as of Dec. 14, 2026, and regularly reside in the Kivalliq region.




KIA is the designated Inuit organization under the Nunavut Final Agreement and one of three regional Inuit organizations associated with Nunavut Tunngavik Inc.

Officers arrived on scene at 1 a.m. following a report of gunfire and located a man “with injuries consistent with a gunshot wound,” the release said.




The victim was transported to the local health centre, where he was pronounced dead.




Police arrested a youth and the Nunavut RCMP Major Crime Unit laid charges that same day.




The youth, whose identity is protected by law, is in custody and scheduled to appear in court in Iqaluit on Nov. 16.




It’s unclear what, if any, relation there is between the accused and victim.
















RCMP are not providing any further details, the release said.

ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ, ᑭᐅᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔭᕆᑐᔪᓄᑦ ᐊᑲᐅᙱᓕᐅᕈᑕᐅᔪᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᕐᔪᐊᒥ, ᐅᖃᐅᓯᐅᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ ᑲᑐᔾᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᒥ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 30−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᑎᓕᐅᖅᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᓕᐊᕆ ᐅᐊᑦᒧᑦ, ᐅᖓᕙ ᑐᓚᑦᑕᕕᒃ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᕕᖓᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓂ; ᐊᒻᒪᔭᓇᕗ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ−ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ, ᓄᓇᕕᖕᒥ ᐊᕕᒃᑐᖅᓯᒪᓂᐅᔪᓂ ᑲᑎᒪᔨᐅᔪᓂ ᐋᓐᓂᐊᖃᕐᓇᙱᑦᑐᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓄᓕᕆᔨᒃᑯᓐᓂ ᐃᓱᒻᒥᖅᑐᐃᔨᖓᓐᓂ.




“ᓅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᒋᐊᖅᓯᒪᕗᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᔪᓯᓂᐊᖅᐳᑦ ᑭᓯᐊᓂ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᓅᑕᐅᕌᓂᒃᐸᑕ,” ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᖅᓯᒪᕗᖅ.




ᓅᑕᐅᓂᖓ ᐃᓚᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᐱᖓᓱᐃᓕᖓᔪᒥ ᐊᖏᕈᑕᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᒥᔪᒥᒃ Argyle Inc.−ᑯᑦ ᐊᑯᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐸᖅᑭᕝᕕᐅᔪᒥ, ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒥ ᐃᓄᑐᖃᕐᓄᑦ ᐊᖏᕐᕋᐅᔪᒥ ᒪᓐᑐᕆᐋᓪ ᓯᓚᑎᑦᑎᐊᖓᓂ ᐳᐊᐃᓐᑦ ᑭᓕᐊᕐᒥ.




“ᐊᖏᕈᑎ ᑐᕌᕋᓱᐊᖅᐳᖅ ᑐᓂᓯᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᑦᑕᓇᙱᑦᑐᒥ, ᐸᖅᑭᑦᑎᐊᖅᑐᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᓕᖅᑯᓯᒧᑦ ᐊᒃᑐᐃᓂᖃᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐆᒪᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᐊᕙᑎᐅᔪᒥ, ᐃᓚᖃᖅᑐᒥ ᐃᓛᓐᓂᓚᐅᓱᖓᕐᒥ ᐊᑐᐃᓐᓇᖃᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖅᑯᓯᑐᖃᖅᑎᒍᑦ ᓂᕿᓂᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐃᑲᔪᖅᓱᐃᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᖓᓱᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓂ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᓂ,” ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐊᖑᔪᖅ ᑲᔪᓯᕗᖅ.




ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᖃᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᓅᑕᐅᒍᑎᒃ, ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᒃ ᒪᑐᓂᐊᖅᐳᖅ.
















ᐅᐊᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᒥᐅᓂᒃ-ᐅᐊᑦᑭᓐᔅ ᑕᒪᒃᑭᑦ ᐊᐅᓪᓚᖅᓯᒪᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ ᓄᓇᓕᖕᓂ ᐅᒃᑐᐱᕆ 1−ᒥ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᖃᐅᓯᒃᓴᓕᐅᕈᓐᓇᙱᖦᖢᑎᒃ, ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᐅᔪᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᖓᑕ ᑲᑐᔾᔨᖃᑎᒌᖑᔪᓂ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᑦ.




ᑰᔾᔪᐊᕐᒥ, ᓯᕗᓪᓕᐅᔪᒥ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᖅᑕᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖑᕙᓪᓕᐊᕗᖅ ᖃᐅᔨᓴᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐱᔪᓐᓇᕋᔭᕐᓂᖓᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐊᖏᓂᖓᓂ ᑎᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᕐᒥ ᑐᓵᔨᐊᐱᖕᒥ ᒫᓐᓇᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐊᑐᒐᒃᓴᐃᑦ ᐋᖅᑭᒃᑕᐅᓯᒪᓂᖓᓐᓄᑦ, ᑐᓴᒐᒃᓴᓕᐊᖅ ᐅᖃᓚᐅᖅᐳᖅ. ᐊᑭᖓᓂ ᓇᓚᐅᑦᑖᕆᔭᐅᓂᐅᔪᒥ ᓂᕆᐅᒋᔭᐅᕗᖅ ᖃᖓᒃᑲᓐᓂᖅ ᑕᒪᑐᒪᓂ ᐅᑭᐅᖑᔪᒥ.

He noted, “We were employed today preparing a place in the vessel’s hold for the Esquimaux to live during the passage to Greenland.”

title: Supreme Court delivers landmark decision on Indigenous offenders and victims
content:
A Supreme Court of Canada decision on Friday has clarified the factors that judges should account for when a defendant and victim are both Indigenous.




The landmark case, 

R. v. Cope

, concerns Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaw man from Nova Scotia who pleaded guilty to assaulting his partner, a Mi’kmaw woman, in 2021.




The Supreme Court weighed in on a trial judge’s decision to sentence Cope to five years in prison and the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s decision to reduce that sentence to three years.




On Friday, the Supreme Court upheld the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal’s ruling, which accounted for Cope’s mental illness and substance use.




“The sentencing judge should have linked the mental health factor to the offender’s moral blameworthiness on the aggravated assault offence, but failed to do so,” wrote Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin, writing for the majority of the judges. “The court of appeal was therefore correct to intervene and it arrived at a just and appropriate sentence.”




Four of nine judges sided with the Nova Scotia provincial court’s original ruling, which dismissed recommendations from community members who proposed no further jail time and opted for a treatment program instead.

Five accessible elders vans that were purchased with $1 million in public money remain off the roads one year after a

The project stalled in 2025, at the end of the previous government’s term, due to a lack of an operating budget.

ᐅᓇ $75-ᒥᓕᐊᓐᑖᓚᑐᕐᑐᖅ, ᐊᖏᓂᖃᖅᖢᓂ 64,500-ᑭᑉᐹᕆᒃᑎᓯᒪᔪᓂ ᕘᑦᓂ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃᓴᖅ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᐅᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ 60 ᐳᓴᓐᑎᒥ ᐱᒋᐊᕈᑎᖃᖅᖢᑎᒃ ᓯᑎᐱᕆ 23-ᖑᑎᓪᓗᒍ, ᐅᖃᓚᐅᕐᑐᖅ ᓴᒃᑯᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᕐᒧᑦ ᑐᑭᒧᐊᖅᑎᑦᑎᔨᖓ ᔭᐃᓴᓐ ᒋᐸᓐᔅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ. ᑕᖅᑭᑦ 18 ᐃᓗᐊᒍᑦ ᐅᓇ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖏᓐᓂᑦ ᑕᒪᒃᑮᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᕐᑐᖅ ᓴᓇᕙᒡᓗᑎᒃ 40-ᓂ ᐃᓚᒌᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑲᑎᕐᖓᐅᖅᑐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓂ ᐊᕐᕌᒍᒥ.




ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐊᕐᕕᐊᓂᒃ ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᕘᓇ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᓄᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᐃᒃᒥ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ (ᐊᔾᔨᙳᐊᖅ ᐅᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᑕᓃᔅ ᑯᓱᒐᖅ/ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᑯᐊᐳᕇᓴᓐᑯᓐᓂᑦ)




ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᖅ 15-ᓂ, 14 ᐃᓅᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᑭᐅᕈᓕᓐ ᓅᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᔨ ᐊᖓᔪᖅᑳᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᖃᓄᐃᓕᐅᕈᑎᖏᓐᓄᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕈᑎᒃᑯᑦ, ᐱᓕᕆᐊᕆᔭᐅᔪᖅ ᐅᑯᓄᖓ ᓴᒃᑯ ᐃᑲᔫᑎᓕᕆᔨᓄᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᑯᐸᒃᒥᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᖅᑎᓄᑦ RG Solution-ᑯᓐᓄᑦ, ᐊᐅᓚᑕᐅᓪᓗᓂ ᐃᓄᖕᓄᑦ ᓇᖕᒥᓂᕆᔭᐅᔪᒧᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃᒥ. ᑖᒃᑯᓇᙵᑦ ᖁᓕᑦ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᖅᐸᒃᑐᑦ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᑦᑎᓂᒃᑰᖓᙱᖢᑎᒃ.




“ᐊᑕᐅᓯᑐᐊᕐᒥ ᐃᓅᙱᑦᑐᒥ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑎᖃᕐᑐᑦ, ᐅᕙᓐᓂ,” ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ ᐊᐱᕐᓱᖅᑕᐅᑎᓪᓗᒍ.




2028 ᐊᕐᕌᒍ ᑎᑭᑉᐸᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔭᖅᑐᑦ 40-ᐅᓕᕐᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐃᓚᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᐸᒃᑐᓂᑦ, ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᓱᓪᓗᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐅᐊᔭᓕᕆᔨᓂᒃ, ᒋᐸᓐᔅ ᐅᖃᕐᒥᔪᖅ.
















ᐱᔪᓐᓇᐅᑎᖃᓕᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᖅ ᒪᑯᓂᖓ ᕿᔪᓕᕆᔨᓂ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᐊᖃᓪᓚᕆᒃᑐᓂᒃ ᐅᓇ ᑲᒻᐸᓂᐅᔪᖅ ᐃᒡᓗᓕᐅᕐᓂᕐᒥ ᐊᔪᕈᓐᓃᖅᓴᖅᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᖅᑐᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᓕᕆᖃᑎᖃᕐᓗᑎᒃ ᓄᓇᕗᒥᑦ ᓯᓚᑦᑐᖅᓴᕐᕕᒃᒥ ᓇᓗᓇᐃᒃᑯᑎᑖᖅᑎᑕᐅᓇᓱᒡᓗᑎᒃ ᓴᓇᔨᐅᔪᑦ, ᓅᑦ ᐅᖃᕐᑐᖅ.




ᓴᒃᑯᑯᑦ ᐃᓱᒪᔪᑦ ᐃᖅᑲᓇᐃᔮᒃᓴᓂ ᑕᒪᐅᖔᕐᓯᒪᙱᑦᑐᓂ ᓴᖅᑭᑎᑦᑎᓂᐊᕋᓱᒋᓪᓗᑎᒃ ᒪᐅᓇ ᐃᖏᕐᕋᔾᔪᑎᓕᕆᓂᒃᑯᑦ, ᐋᖄᖅᑭᒃᓱᐃᕙᓪᓕᐊᓂᒃᑯᑦ ᐊᒻᒪ ᐱᐊᓂᒃᑕᐅᑎᑦᑎᔾᔪᑎᒃᑯᑦ.




ᒫᓂ ᐊᑕᐅᓯᖅ ᐱᖓᓲᓕᖓᓪᓗᒍ ᐱᓕᕆᕝᕕᒃ, ᑖᓐᓇᓗ ᓴᓇᔭᐅᓕᓚᐅᕐᓯᒪᔪᖅ 2023-ᒥ ᐊᐅᓚᔾᔪᑎ

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Videographer assaulted while filming for Gjoa Haven clean energy initiative
content:
A videographer 

was assaulted Monday in Gjoa Haven while filming for an energy-saving initiative, says Mayor Raymond Quqshuun Sr.




“The hamlet is taking the incident seriously while respecting the privacy of those involved,” Quqshuun said in an email to Nunatsiaq News on Thursday.




It’s unclear what exactly happened but the victim was uninjured, Quqshuun said. The incident was reported to the hamlet but not the RCMP.




The mayor did not say if the victim was visiting the community and declined to provide any further details.




In a Facebook post on Wednesday, the account for the hamlet’s mayor described the victim as a videographer involved in Gjoa Haven’s Winter Clean Energy Challenge, an initiative that encourages households to reduce energy use in the winter.




“Incidents like these are unusual,” Quqshuun said in his email, adding that the community is known to be “particularly warm and welcoming” to guests.




Run by the Kikitak Housing Association, Qulliq Energy Corp., the hamlet maintenance team and Yukon University’s Northern Energy Innovation program, the challenge provides participants with weather-stripping material, window film and energy-friendly shower heads.
















The household with the largest energy reduction wins an electric side-by-side utility terrain vehicle, Quqshuun said.

author: Daron Letts
title: Crosswalk crash stalls Iqaluit traffic
content:
A downed crosswalk pole on Niaqungusiariaq Rd., across from Iqaluit’s Qikiqtani General Hospital clinic entrance, slowed traffic for 90 minutes, following a two-car collision at around noon on Thursday.




“Everyone was checked at the scene, and one person went to the hospital on their own afterwards for further assessment,” said city spokesperson Geoff Byrne in an email.




The city warned drivers of the traffic disruption in a public service announcement issued shortly after 12 p.m.




Two RCMP vehicles blocked Niaqungusiariaq Rd. about two hundred metres past the Sailijaaqvik boarding home at the southeast corner of the intersection. An RCMP truck also blocked Queen Elizabeth Way about 100 metres from the entrance to Astro Hill.




Traffic was backed up on Niaqungusiariaq Road all the way up to Joamie School for approximately 90 minutes while city workers removed the pole, broken in two places, with heavy equipment. The crew also filled-in the hole left behind.




The intersection is the site of Iqaluit’s first controlled 

crosswalk

, which was installed in fall 2024.

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: RCMP arrest suspect in Pangnirtung shooting
content:
The RCMP has arrested a 21-year-old man in relation to a shooting in Pangnirtung on Tuesday afternoon.




Police received reports of gunshots at around 4:03 p.m. Tuesday. Ten minutes later, they arrested Jonah Kuniliusie, according to a news release issued by Sgt. George Henrie on Thursday.




Kuniliusie faces two counts of endangering life, two counts of pointing a firearm, two counts of aggravated assault, and the unlawful possession of a weapon in public. He also faces three counts for breach of probation.




The RCMP was not immediately available to answer questions about the incident.




Deputy mayor Markus Wilcke said the event harmed everyone in the community, either directly or indirectly, including children who were nearby 

when the shooting happened

.




Kuniliusie remains in custody and will have his next court appearance on Oct. 20 in Iqaluit.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala honours leaders, volunteers
content:
Leadership and volunteerism were recognized during the Nunavut Sport and Recreation awards gala at Iqaluit’s Aqsarniit hotel on Saturday.




The Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut co-hosted the event in partnership with the NU Sport Federation and the territorial government’s sport and recreation division.




Novoalia Carriere of Kinngait earned the Calm Air Youth Leader of the Year award for his work as a summer camp supervisor and now as head of the hamlet’s after-school program.




“Sport is important for young people because it promotes healthy physical growth, builds mental resilience, and teaches essential life and social skills,” said Carriere over Facebook Thursday.




The 18-year-old athlete cares for up to 40 children aged five through 12 from 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. weekdays at the youth centre.




With the music of Black Eyed Peas and other pop artists filling the background at low volume, Carriere tries to create an atmosphere that’s distinct from school and home.




He cycles through creative indoor activities to foster social connection without any concern for “competition or adult expectations.”

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Nanuq is king of Arctic-inspired chess set
content:
A men’s group in Cambridge Bay has helped create a Nunavut-inspired chess set that features polar bears, grizzlies, snowy owls, rabbits and muskoxen.




Clifford Nzombato plays an Arctic-inspired Snakes and Ladders game he helped create at the National Arts Centre in Ottawa. The board features northern wildlife. Players who land on an animal’s mouth slide down to its tail. (Photo by Nehaa Bimal)




Hunter Nathan Kaoslead has led the Cambridge Bay men’s group for two years. He said the idea emerged last year as the men played chess, Snakes and Ladders and cards at their weekly game nights.







“As we were playing, we said to each other, ‘Wouldn’t it be awesome if these were Arctic animal pieces?'” Kaoslead said.




Kaoslead first drew the animals on a napkin, then figured out how they could replace traditional chess pieces. He also consulted elders on names and characteristics.




The resulting Isumaniq Chess includes a polar bear, or nanuq in Inuinnaqtun, as the king; a grizzly bear, or akhak, as the queen; a snowy owl, or okpik, as the bishop; a rabbit, or okalik, as the knight; and a muskox, or umingmak, as the rook.




An inuksuk represents the pawns.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New Ungava MNA promises to bring Nunavik to the table
content:
Newly elected Ungava MNA Sonia Caron says her first priority after taking office will be to travel north and begin building relationships with Nunavik’s communities.




Caron, a Parti Québécois candidate and longtime educator from Chibougamau, won the northern riding in Monday’s provincial election with 39.5 per cent of the vote. The PQ formed a minority government, winning 59 of 127 seats in Quebec’s national assembly.




“I feel honored and very proud that the people of Ungava have placed their trust in me for the next term,” Caron said in a French interview Wednesday.




Caron succeeds Coalition Avenir Québec member Denis Lamothe, who represented the riding since 2018. He was a member of the Coalition party’s governments led by former premiers François Legault and Christine Fréchette.

Coalition Avenir Québec, which won elections in 2018 and 2022, was wiped out Monday, losing all it seats across the province.




Caron said she plans to make Nunavik her first official destination once the government’s schedule is established.




She hopes to visit all 14 communities in Nunavik if logistics allow, although she acknowledged that it may require several trips.




“I will be present,” she said.
















The PQ is a separatist party, and its victory has renewed questions about what independence could mean for Indigenous nations and their relationship with the province

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Man injured after shooting in Pangnirtung, deputy mayor says
content:
Pangnirtung is in shock after a shooting Tuesday afternoon injured a man, says deputy Mayor Markus Wilcke.




Wilcke said he heard shots Tuesday at around 4 p.m. and that the RCMP has since made an arrest.




“A lot of people were impacted, many of them children,” the deputy mayor said in an interview. “Pretty well everybody was impacted, directly or indirectly.”




He said the shots came from near the harbour. The suspect then entered residential streets and the area near the hamlet office.




“The RCMP did a good job and everyone is safe now,” Wilcke said.




Nunatsiaq News asked the RCMP about the incident but was told information about it would be available Thursday.




Wilcke says the hamlet will update the community through public statements and that counselling services will be available.
















He also said the community can expect a public meeting within the next few days to discuss what actions are needed to respond and prevent similar incidents in the future.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Boil water advisory issued for Taloyoak
content:
Nunavut’s Health Department issued a boil water advisory for Taloyoak due to the mechanical failure of a pump at the water treatment plant.




Any water used for consumption must be brought to a rolling boil for a minimum of one minute, either on the stove or with a kettle that does not have an automatic shut off, according to the advisory.




The advisory applies to water for drinking, preparing infant formulas, making juice or ice cubes, washing produce, cooking and brushing teeth.




Residents are also reminded that a camp stove should be used outdoors to avoid the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.




The Health Department will notify community members when the boil advisory has been lifted.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut duo wins at Pan-Arctic Vision
content:
A duo from Nunavut earned one of three honours at the fourth-annual Pan-Arctic Vision competition in Denmark on Oct. 2.




Christine Piunguałaq Tootoo

 of Rankin Inlet and 

Tooma Laisa

 of Iqaluit shared the award for “most feeling of community and togetherness.” 




The event, billed as the Arctic’s answer to the Eurovision Song Contest, took place at the Nordic House in Tórshavn, Faroe Islands.




“I love experiencing new cultures and languages,” Tootoo said in a preprepared video broadcast before her performance alongside Laisa. “Travelling gives me a zest for life.”




Travel was the theme of their traditional drum song, 

Kiviuq

.




Kiviuq is the name of a 

legendary Inuk

 who travelled across “the imaginary borders” of Inuit Nunangat, Tootoo said as she introduced the song from the stage.




Laisa softly drummed and hummed beside Tootoo, who recorded and looped Laisa’s voice. Then they sang their rendition of the legend.
















When the performance ended, the audience broke the silence with a roar of applause.




Icelandic rock band Falinn gjóður won “most revolutionary song” and Nuunu, a Greenlandic singer-songwriter who goes by one name, won “most Arctic song.”

title: Ottawa gives $77M to Arctic Bay for small craft harbour
content:
The federal government has announced $77-million in funding for a multi-use small craft harbour to be built in Arctic Bay.




The harbour will include a breakwater, launch ramp, fixed wharf for larger vessels, floating wharves for small craft vessels, dredging for the harbour basin and an entrance channel, according to a Fisheries and Oceans Canada press release issued on Oct. 2.




“This harbour will create opportunities for hunters, fishers and families to be more independent. Food sovereignty and economic prosperity will follow,” said Nunavut MP Lori Idlout in the release.




Construction began in August and will continue until 2029. It’s expected to be operational for the following open water season.




Pilitak Enterprises Ltd., an Inuit-owned construction company based in Iqaluit, is the contractor.




The contract created between the company and the hamlet includes an Inuit benefits plan to support local training and employment.




According to the release, the federal government is continuing to work with northern communities to help with development and create more resources for residents of the north such as this new harbour.

author: Randi Beers
title: Baffinland seeks court approval for sale of assets
content:
Baffinland Iron Mines Corp. is seeking court approval to solicit bids on its shares and assets, which may include its Mary River Mine.




The company operates the mine on north Baffin Island and touts its ore as some of the highest-grade in the world. It began operations in 2014.




Baffinland 

sought creditor protection

The company

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Cambridge Bay helps keep Northwest Passage expedition moving
content:
A handful of bolts and a little help from Cambridge Bay residents kept a Polish sailing crew from being stranded in the Canadian Arctic.




Captains Alicja Latoń and Andrzej Górajek, who work for the Polish cruise and expedition company Natango, arrived in Cambridge Bay on Sept. 12 with a damaged propulsion system and were stuck for about a week.







Alicja Latoń, left, and Andrzej Górajek, right, crew members of the Polish sailing yacht Ocean A, stand ashore in Erebus Bay on Sept. 21, during the yacht’s eastbound return through the Canadian Northwest Passage. (Photo by Andrzej Górajek)




“It became the place that determined whether the entire second half of the expedition would be possible at all,” Górajek said in an email to Nunatsiaq News.




The pair is attempting to complete a trip that began July 29 with seven crew members. Their goal is to sail the Canadian section of the Northwest Passage in a single navigation season, from Upernavik, Greenland, to Tuktoyaktuk and back to Maniitsoq, Greenland.




“We wanted to find out whether a small sailing yacht could make the passage in both directions without wintering in between,” said Górajek, who is completing the return trip with Latoń.




The crew is calling the expedition, on the 75-foot Ocean A yacht, the “first known and documented” voyage rather than the first-ever, because historical records may be incomplete.

title: PQ’s Sonia Caron takes Ungava as her party wins minority government
content:
Nunavimmiut will be represented by Parti Québécois candidate Sonia Caron, who was elected Monday in Quebec’s geographically largest riding.




The PQ won a minority government in Monday’s provincial election, taking the largest number of seats in Quebec’s national assembly.




In Ungava, the massive riding that includes Nunavik and other parts of northern Quebec, Caron got 3,312 votes — 39.5 per cent of ballots cast, according to Élections Québec’s website.




Caron, originally from Chibougamau, is the director of professional development at the Centre de services scolaire de la Baie-James, which oversees trades programs in northern Quebec. She described herself in an 

interview

 last week as a lifelong supporter of the PQ.




She had a 25-year career in education before making the jump to politics this year after she was approached by several parties to be their candidate.




Caron told Nunatsiaq News she got into politics because the lack of front-line health services and the need for clean drinking water in many remote communities need urgent attention.




“I told myself, ‘We have to do something,’ because our region is undergoing major upheavals, and public services are constantly deteriorating,” Caron said in an interview before the election.
















Liberal Sandrine Rious finished second in the five-way race, taking 2,308 votes, or 27.5 per cent of ballots

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Quebec election day goes smoothly in Nunavik, officials say
content:
Officials say voting in the Ungava riding during Quebec’s provincial election is unfolding with no issues — a stark contrast from the 2025 federal election.




Polling stations are open in every community in the region, with two elections officers in each community, said Élections Québec spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet in an email on Monday.




From Sept. 26 to Sept. 30, the advance polling dates in Nunavik, election staff helped residents get on the electors list to participate in the election, she said.




Election staff also recruited and trained locals to run the election, she added.

title: Jason Iqaluq prepares to head to Iqaluit after byelection win
content:
Jason Iqaluq said Friday he was preparing to head to Iqaluit, after having been elected to represent Hudson Bay in Nunavut’s legislative assembly.




He said he found out the results of the byelection around 9 p.m. on Sept. 28, while relaxing at home and playing video games. Voting took place at the council chamber in Sanikiluaq, the sole community represented under the Hudson Bay riding.




“I was trying to keep my mind busy,” he said in a phone interview Friday, adding it was a pleasant surprise to find out he won.




Iqaluq has lived in Sanikiluaq his entire life. He’ll now commit himself full-time to politics, after working as a team leader at the airport and serving on the board of his local Arctic Co-op.




The trip from Sanikiluaq to Iqaluit was expected to be a long one, Iqaluq said, since he had to first fly from the island community in Hudson Bay to Winnipeg and stay overnight before he could catch a flight to Iqaluit on Sunday.




“I’m a bit anxious, but overall, I’m feeling that I can do this,” he said about the journey ahead.




He said his MLA orientation should begin this week and that he expects to be sworn in formally at the legislative assembly by the end of October.

On August 13, 1877, an unusual expedition left New London, Conn., bound for Cumberland Sound on the southeastern coast of Baffin Island. Known officially as the Howgate Preliminary Arctic Expedition, it was to be the first stage of a much grander enterprise planned by Captain Henry W. Howgate of the United States Army.




Howgate had been inspired by the recent British expedition to the High Arctic led by George Nares. With two ships, Nares had tried to reach the North Pole by way of Smith Sound, the narrow channel separating Ellesmere Island from Greenland. One ship, the Alert, had reached a point on Ellesmere Island farther north than any other ship had ever gone and wintered there.




Howgate thought that Americans should do one better than the British. He wanted to establish a permanent scientific colony at Lady Franklin Bay. For that, he would need Inuit — for he knew that none lived that far north — and dogs and skin clothing.




And so a plan was hatched that a preliminary expedition would travel to Cumberland Sound and winter there. It would be under the command of Captain George Tyson, a whaler well known to the Inuit of the sound. title: Education must continue to be the counter to denialism
content:
Education remains the best way to ensure Canadians understand the legacy of residential schools, to preserve the memories of children who died, and to care for survivors.




Earlier this week, after the Second Sons white nationalist group held an ominous demonstration just outside the Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc reserve near Kamloops, B.C., it became easier to understand the calls to criminalize residential school denialism.




A recurring theme at the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation ceremony on Parliament Hill, residential school denialism is becoming an alarming, disturbing phenomenon.




“We must … confront all forms of denialism that persist despite extensive historical records and an indisputable body of evidence, including first-hand survivor testimony,” Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said during Wednesday’s event. “This leaves no room for doubt about the history and impact of the residential schools.”




Several speakers spoke to the harms caused by denialism, which is the belief that either children didn’t die at residential schools or that survivors’ experiences were not as bad as they have made it out to be.

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Nunavut sports hall of fame inductions begin
content:
The Nunavut Sport Federation will induct its hall of fame’s inaugural class this weekend at the Aqsarniit hotel in Iqaluit.




The ceremony will take place during the Sport and Recreation Awards gala, where the Government of Nunavut recognizes the territory’s athletes, administrators, volunteers and coaches, according to a news release issued Friday by the Recreation and Parks Association of Nunavut.




Former NHL player Jordin Tootoo and Inuit games athlete Attima Hadlari are the first inductees into the hall.




Doors open to the gala at 6:30 p.m. The ceremony begins at 7 p.m.




From 2003 to 2017, Tootoo, played 723 games for the Nashville Predators, Detroit Red Wings, New Jersey Devils and Chicago Blackhawks. He racked up 65 goals, 96 assists and 1,010 penalty minutes during that time.




Hadlari was an Arctic sports athlete from Cambridge Bay who mastered the sealskin whip and went on to coach and officiate for young athletes participating in traditional Inuit games.




He also served in the first Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit Katimajiit, which gives expertise in how to apply Inuit traditional knowledge in government, from 2003 to 2005.
















Each year, the Nunavut Sports and Recreation Hall of Fame plans to take nominations from community members for inductees.

author: Randi Beers
title: The people we carry with us
content:
Annie Qimirpik




There are some people you expect to see forever. You see them around town, talk to them, tease each other, make plans without thinking too much about whether those plans will happen.




Because why wouldn’t they? When you live in a small community, people become part of the landscape of your life. You know where they live; that is their family. You recognize their voice before you see them.




And then suddenly they’re not there anymore.




I think one of the strangest things about grief is how ordinary the world continues to feel.




The sun is still rising. People still go to work. Kids still play outside. Planes come and go.




Life doesn’t stop just because someone you love is no longer living it with you.
















That can feel unfair, confusing and sometimes angering.




In a small community, loss is rarely experienced alone. When some dies, their absence can be part of the community itself.




There’s an empty place where they used to sit.




A name that comes up in conversation, a story someone tells, a song that suddenly means something: g

rief has a strange way of making ordinary things significant.




Sometimes, we talk so much about how someone died that we forget how they lived.

Marc Damant says he wants to represent Ungava because Nunavik needs a local representative in the Quebec national assembly.




“I think it’s time that Nunavik had someone who was more of a full-time MNA,” said Damant, who lives in Kuujjuaq and is the Quebec Conservative party’s candidate in the Oct. 5 provincial election.




He said that previous MNAs didn’t enough of an interest in the region, and that people feel like they don’t matter.




While he acknowledged logistical and financial challenges make it difficult for candidates to visit Nunavik’s villages, he said nothing beats face-to-face conversation with electors.




“We have to do better for everyone,” said Damant, adding he’s the only candidate with posters up in Kuujjuaq right now.




Damant works as an airport manager for the Kativik Regional Government, where he’s responsible for airport operations and safety for multiple communities across Nunavik. From 2007 to 2014, he was a grounds operations co-ordinator for Air Inuit, a role that allowed him to travel across Nunavik.
















He also spent 11 years as a reservist in the Canadian Armed Forces and previously taught in China, Akulivik and La Tabatier

title: Iqaluit’s low-barrier shelter to open in January
content:
Uquutaq Society’s new $40-million low-barrier shelter is slated to open in Iqaluit in January.




The new building is located downtown at 158 Nipisa St., near The Snack Restaurant.




Uquutaq Society’s emerging new three-storey facility includes 44 low-barrier shelter beds on the second floor and 13 single-room transitional housing units on the top floor. The main floor will be a warming centre during the day. (Photo by Daron Letts)




“This is a low-barrier site, meaning you don’t need to be sober or unimpaired [to enter],” said society CEO Laurel McCorriston in an interview in September.




Named by elders as Ullivik, which means “the place you wait for the tide,” the three-storey, 44-bed facility will offer

couples, which can also serve as private space for individuals in need of quiet or privacy.




The building includes an additional 13 single-occupancy transitional housing units on the top floor.




Currently, the only other low-barrier facility in the city is the society’s 17-cot overnight shelter at 534 Niaqunngusiariaq Road, which accommodates five women and 12 men nightly.

content:

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Nunavik beneficiaries to see a 25% gas subsidy increase
content:
The Kativik Regional Government and Makivvik increased the gasoline subsidy for Inuit beneficiaries nearly 25 per cent Thursday.




The subsidy went to $1 per litre from 78 cents, following an a 32-cent jump in gasoline prices, according to a joint press release issued Wednesday.




“Gasoline in Nunavik is not a luxury. It is what allows people to get out on the land, harvest food, visit family and move within their communities,” Makivvik president Pita Aatami said in the release.




The subsidy is available for James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement beneficiaries.




Before the price and subsidy increases, beneficiaries were paying $1.69 per litre of gas. Now they will pay $1.78.




This subsidy is part of a wider suite of “cost-of-living” subsidies, to which the provincial government recently promised $155 million over the next six years, according to the release.




The other five subsidies impact food, airfare, harvesting equipment, elder assistance and household appliances.

title: I’m growing older than my anaanatsiaq will ever be
content:
Not everyone has the privilege of growing up with their grandparents presence and knowledge. It’s a blessing I didn’t have.




My anaanatsiaq was Tookasie Akpaleeapik. When my family, who is from Pond Inlet, was chosen to help the Inujjuarmiut (families from Inukjuak) adjust during the High Arctic Relocation in the 1950s, she followed to Grise Fiord.




Author Larry Audlaluk mentions my grandmother in his memoir 

What I Remember, What I Know: The Life of a High Arctic Exile

.




“When we arrived in Grise, after the aircraft’s engines stopped and the pilot opened the door to let us out, none of us wanted to be the first to get out. We were too shy. Tookashie was the brave one, getting out first.”




After the relocation she was sent to Churchill, Man., where she attended residential school. After graduation, Tookasie Akpaleeapik moved to Ottawa to practise nursing.




She took her own life shortly after, and that loss still affects my family. Grief doesn’t just magically go away over time; it stays with us throughout generations.




Everyone remembers her as a strong young woman who wasn’t scared to follow her dreams, regardless of hardships.
















Her soul is still shining bright through my oldest sister, Maggie Tookasie, who was given my anaanatsiaq’s name by my anaana (mother) Katie Koonoo.
